key_insight: A stool microbiome-based risk score built from 28 microbial species was associated with a higher future risk of cancer diagnosis years after sampling.
clinical_relevance: This suggests the gut microbiome could help flag people at higher cancer risk for earlier risk stratification, though it is not yet ready for clinical use.
method: Shotgun metagenomic sequencing of stool from 5,997 participants in population cohorts.
Built a microbiome-derived risk score using 28 microbial species.
Tested the score against incident cancer over up to 10 years and in independent external datasets.
evidence_signal: In the discovery cohorts, each 1-SD increase in the score was linked to higher incident cancer risk (adjusted HR 1.62, 95% CI 1.44-1.82), and the score also separated cancer cases from controls in 1,879 cases and 5,341 controls.
watch_item: The findings are associative and need prospective validation before the score can be used reliably for screening or decision-making.
paper_title: A gut microbiome-derived risk score is associated with future cancer development
